title: The ADO Connection Object
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of the ado connection object in a Classic ASP application.
Identify and describe at least two syllabus subtopics: Creating an ADODB.Connection and Opening a database connection.
Inspect a minimal example and define a reproducible normal-case and failure-case test.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study the ado connection object as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 67 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: The ADO Connection Object matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Classic ASP applications commonly use ADO to access relational databases through a provider. For 'The ADO Connection Object', validate inputs, prefer `ADODB.Command` parameters for values, close Recordsets and Connections, and handle failures without exposing the query, connection string, or database details. Parameter syntax, supported types, cursor behavior, and connection string details can vary by provider; verify them against the installed driver and database.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Creating an ADODB.Connection; Opening a database connection; Connection string configuration; Connection timeout settings; Handling connection errors; Closing connections; Managing connection lifetime. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: The ADO Connection Object
content_blocks.code:
<%
Dim conn
Set conn = Server.CreateObject("ADODB.Connection")
conn.ConnectionTimeout = 10
' conn.ConnectionString = ReadProtectedConnectionString()  ' application-defined
' conn.Open
' ... use the connection ...
' conn.Close
Set conn = Nothing
%>
content_blocks.expected_output: A Connection object is created with a bounded connection timeout.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use synthetic records in a local test database and a least-privilege database account. Record the database/provider version and verify both success and failure cases. The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

content_blocks.title: Guided workflow
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with a minimal local example of the ado connection object. 2. Trace its inputs, state changes, dependencies, and output. 3. Test a normal case, a missing/malformed case, and one permission/provider/runtime failure. 4. Write down the exact expected and observed result before changing another variable.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.
